lead: Perfect secrecy is a strict promise: after seeing the ciphertext, an attacker's belief about the message does not change. The one-time pad reaches this promise with one XOR: c = m ⊕ k, where k is a truly random key as long as m and is used once. Only a few universities teach this material, so treat it as advanced. The idea matters because it is the benchmark for practical ciphers, and its limits—long keys, secure key distribution, no integrity—explain why real systems use stream and block ciphers.
prereq: You need: basic XOR from digital logic, and the cipher notation from Chapter 3.1.

blocks.text: Perfect secrecy is defined with probabilities. Let M be the message random variable and C the ciphertext random variable. A cipher is perfectly secret when the ciphertext gives no information about the message.
Pr[M = m | C = c] = Pr[M = m]
blocks.where: M is the message random variable, C is the ciphertext random variable, m is any message with Pr[M = m] > 0, and c is any ciphertext with Pr[C = c] > 0.

blocks.text: Read the bar as 'given'. The left side is the attacker's belief about message m after seeing ciphertext c. The right side is the belief before seeing c. Equality says the ciphertext does not change the belief. It must hold for every m and c that can occur.

This is an information-theoretic condition, not a computing-time condition. The attacker may have unlimited computing power. Perfect secrecy requires a key at least as long as the message and uniformly random; this is the limit that makes the one-time pad special.
The one-time pad encrypts a bit string by XOR. Write m for the message bits and k for the key bits, both of length n. Encryption is c = m ⊕ k. Decryption is m = c ⊕ k, because (m ⊕ k) ⊕ k = m.
c = m ⊕ k,   m = c ⊕ k
blocks.where: m is the message bit string, k is the key bit string of the same length, c is the ciphertext bit string, and ⊕ is bitwise XOR.

blocks.text: Take k uniform over {0,1}ⁿ: each n-bit key has probability 1/2ⁿ. Fix m and c. Exactly one key maps m to c, namely k = m ⊕ c. So Pr[C = c | M = m] = 1/2ⁿ. Then Pr[C = c] = Σₘ Pr[M = m] × 1/2ⁿ = 1/2ⁿ. Bayes' rule gives Pr[M = m | C = c] = Pr[C = c | M = m] Pr[M = m] / Pr[C = c] = Pr[M = m]. This is perfect secrecy.
Reuse breaks the pad. If c₁ = m₁ ⊕ k and c₂ = m₂ ⊕ k, then c₁ ⊕ c₂ = m₁ ⊕ m₂. The key disappears, and the attacker learns the XOR of the two messages.

Limits: k must be as long as m, truly random, shared over a secure channel, and never reused. The pad gives confidentiality only. An attacker can flip chosen bits of c and the same flips appear in m; integrity needs a MAC or authenticated encryption (see Unit 4). A stream cipher that expands a short seed is not a one-time pad; see Chapter 3.3.

figure.caption: XORing m = 1011 with the key 0110 gives c = 1101 (13); XORing c with the same key gives back 1011 (11). Because the key is random and used once, the ciphertext reveals nothing about the message.

spec.aria: Four rows of four bit cells: message 1011, key 0110, ciphertext 1101 and the decryption 1011, with their decimal values 11, 6, 13 and 11.

examples.question: A one-time pad uses the 4-bit key k = 0110. The message is m = 1011. (a) Find the ciphertext c = m ⊕ k. (b) Decrypt c with the same key. (c) Give the decimal values of m, k, and c.
steps: Write both strings with four bits: m = 1011₂ and k = 0110₂.
Decimal check: m = 11, k = 6, c = 13, and 13 ⊕ 6 = 11.
examples.answer: The ciphertext is 1101₂ (13), and decryption returns 1011₂ (11).

traps: Perfect secrecy is not computational security: the attacker may have unlimited computing power.
The key must be truly random, as long as the message, and used once. A short seed stretched by a PRG is not a one-time pad.
Never reuse a pad: c₁ ⊕ c₂ = m₁ ⊕ m₂ removes the key.
OTP gives confidentiality only; bit flips in c appear in m, so integrity needs a MAC (Unit 4).

quiz.a: Pr[M = m | C = c] = Pr[M = m] for all m and c with nonzero probability.

quiz.q: Why does a uniform key make every ciphertext equally likely for a fixed message?
quiz.a: For each ciphertext c there is exactly one key k = m ⊕ c, so that key has probability 1/2ⁿ.

quiz.q: m = 1011, k = 0110. Find c and the decrypted message.
Two messages use the same pad. c₁ = 1101 and c₂ = 1110. What does the attacker learn?
quiz.a: c₁ ⊕ c₂ = 0011 = m₁ ⊕ m₂, so the attacker learns the XOR of the two messages and the key is removed.

quiz.q: Give two limitations of the one-time pad.
quiz.a: The key is as long as the message and must be distributed securely; it also gives no integrity.

quiz.q: Why is a stream cipher with a short seed not a one-time pad?
quiz.a: Its keystream is not truly random and repeats if the seed repeats; the key is not as long as the message.

beyond: Not for the exam. The one-time pad is a benchmark in information-theoretic security and is used in a few ultra-secure links. Practical systems use stream ciphers (Chapter 3.3) or block cipher modes (Chapter 3.7) because they expand a short key. Quantum key distribution can supply random keys, but authentication and integrity still need separate mechanisms; see Unit 4. Search for Shannon secrecy, pad reuse attacks, and information-theoretic security.
